---
title: "Function Reference"
subtitle: "Public API for taxodist 1.0.0 in R, Python, and Julia."
---

The R, Python, and Julia implementations share the same distance semantics and principal function names. Native return types follow the conventions of each language.

| Concept | R | Python | Julia |
|---|---|---|---|
| Missing scalar result | `NULL` or `NA` | `None` or `NaN` | `nothing` or `NaN` |
| Distance matrix | Base R `dist` | `pandas.DataFrame` | `TaxonomicDistanceMatrix` |
| Structured result | S3 list or data frame | `dict` or `pandas.DataFrame` | Named tuple or `DataFrame` |
| Cache file | `.rds` | `.pkl` | `.json` |

Unless stated otherwise, retrieval functions accept `verbose = FALSE` in R and `verbose=false` in Python and Julia. Queried names are normalized (surrounding and repeated whitespace) before lookup.

Functions that compute distances accept `metric = "reciprocal"` (the default), `"path"`, `"wu_palmer"`, or `"ranked"`; see [`taxo_distance()`](#taxo_distance) for the definitions.

### Settings

| Setting | Default | R | Python | Julia |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Attempts per request (retried with exponential backoff after network errors and 5xx responses) | 3 | `options(taxodist.max_tries = n)` | `taxodist.fetch.MAX_TRIES = n` | `Taxodist.MAX_TRIES[] = n` |
| Minimum interval between consecutive requests, in seconds (0 disables it) | 0.25 | `options(taxodist.min_interval = s)` | `taxodist.fetch.MIN_INTERVAL = s` | `Taxodist.MIN_INTERVAL[] = s` |
| Rank levels used by `metric = "ranked"` | kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species | `options(taxodist.rank_levels = ...)` | `taxodist.distance.RANK_LEVELS = [...]` | `Taxodist.RANK_LEVELS[] = [...]` |
| Persistent cache directory | per-user cache directory | `tools::R_user_dir("taxodist", "cache")` | `TAXODIST_CACHE_DIR` | `TAXODIST_CACHE_DIR` |

## Taxon retrieval and search

### `taxonomicon_available()`

```text
R:      taxonomicon_available(timeout = 3)
Python: taxonomicon_available(timeout=3)
Julia:  taxonomicon_available(; timeout=3)
```

Sends a single quick request to The Taxonomicon and reports whether it answered. Useful to skip code that needs the server, such as examples, when there is no internet connection or the server is down; lineage retrieval itself already handles failed requests.

**Returns:** `TRUE`/`True`/`true` if the server answered with a successful response, otherwise false.

### `get_taxonomicon_id()`

```text
R:      get_taxonomicon_id(taxon, verbose = FALSE)
Python: get_taxonomicon_id(taxon, verbose=False)
Julia:  get_taxonomicon_id(taxon; verbose=false)
```

Resolves a taxon name to a numeric Taxonomicon identifier. Astronomical entries are excluded. When several valid biological entries remain, the function warns before returning the first candidate.

**Returns:** a character string in R, `str` in Python, or `String` in Julia; `NULL`/`None`/`nothing` if no valid identifier is found or the server cannot be reached.

### `get_lineage_by_id()`

```text
R:      get_lineage_by_id(taxon_id, clean = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
Python: get_lineage_by_id(taxon_id, clean=True, verbose=False)
Julia:  get_lineage_by_id(taxon_id; clean=true, verbose=false)
```

Retrieves an ordered lineage for one numeric Taxonomicon ID, supplied as a string or a number. Formatting markers are always removed; with `clean` enabled, nodes preceding `Biota` are also removed. Cleaned and uncleaned lineages are cached separately, and supplying several IDs is an error.

**Returns:** a character vector in R, list of strings in Python, or `Vector{String}` in Julia, ordered from root to queried node; `NULL`/`None`/`nothing` for an invalid or unresolved ID.

### `get_lineage()`

```text
R:      get_lineage(taxon, clean = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
Python: get_lineage(taxon, clean=True, verbose=False)
Julia:  get_lineage(taxon; clean=true, verbose=false)
```

Convenience wrapper combining name resolution and lineage retrieval. A numeric ID bypasses name search. For names, the lineage is truncated at the queried taxon, which is located exactly and, failing that, without regard to letter case.

**Returns:** a character vector in R, list of strings in Python, or `Vector{String}` in Julia; `NULL`/`None`/`nothing` if unresolved.

Lineages are read from the structured hierarchy of the Taxonomicon page: each node is the scientific name marked up by the page itself, so author strings, rank labels, and extinction or type markers are not part of node names. Pages without that block are parsed from text by extracting the scientific name at the start of each line.

### `lineage_ranks()`

```text
R:      lineage_ranks(taxon, clean = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
Python: lineage_ranks(taxon, clean=True, verbose=False)
Julia:  lineage_ranks(taxon; clean=true, verbose=false)
```

Returns each node of the lineage of a taxon together with its rank in The Taxonomicon classification (for example `"Kingdom"`, `"Clade"`, `"Superfamily"`, or `"Genus"`). The nodes are exactly those returned by `get_lineage()` for the same arguments. Ranks are read from the label preceding each name, without the `[crown]`, `[plesion]`, and `[stem]` qualifiers or extinction markers; rows without a label are species, subspecies, or subgenera, whose rank is inferred from the form of the name. Many nodes are unranked clades (`"Clade"`).

**Returns:** a data frame with columns `node`, `rank`, and `depth`, one row per node from root to tip; `rank` is missing (`NA`/`None`/`missing`) for nodes without a stated rank. `NULL`/`None`/`nothing` if the taxon cannot be found.

### `taxo_search()`

```text
R:      taxo_search(taxon, verbose = FALSE)
Python: taxo_search(taxon, verbose=False)
Julia:  taxo_search(taxon; verbose=false)
```

Lists biological Taxonomicon search results after removing astronomical entries and duplicate identifiers.

**Returns:** a data frame with columns `id` and `name`, or `NULL`/`None` when no matches are found.

::: {.callout-note title="Reproducible name resolution"}
For ambiguous names, inspect `taxo_search()` and record the selected numeric ID and retrieval date. The Taxonomicon is external to the package and its classifications may change.
:::

## Auditable resolution and portable bundles

### `taxo_resolve()`

```text
R:      taxo_resolve(taxa, ambiguity = "warn", verbose = FALSE,
                     progress = TRUE, within = NULL)
Python: taxo_resolve(taxa, ambiguity="warn", verbose=False,
                     progress=True, within=None)
Julia:  taxo_resolve(taxa; ambiguity="warn", verbose=false,
                     progress=true, within=nothing)
```

Resolves a complete input vector before analysis. Repeated names, including spellings that differ only in whitespace, retain their original positions but are retrieved only once. Numeric identifiers bypass name search. Selected lineages are truncated exactly as in `get_lineage()`.

`ambiguity` accepts `"warn"`, `"first"`, or `"error"`. Ambiguous rows retain `status = "ambiguous"` even when the first candidate is selected. Candidates marked as invalid, rejected, nude, or illegitimate names (`nom. inval.`, `nom. rej.`, `nom. nud.`, `nom. illeg.`) are considered only after the others. `within` optionally names a clade; only candidates whose lineage contains it (exact, case-insensitive match) are considered, and names without such a candidate are `unresolved`.

**Returns:** a `taxodist_resolution` data frame in R, `TaxodistResolution` in Python, or `TaxodistResolution` wrapping a Julia `DataFrame`. Each input has:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `input` | Original queried label |
| `resolved_name` | Final node of the selected lineage |
| `id` | Selected Taxonomicon or custom identifier |
| `status` | `resolved`, `ambiguous`, `unresolved` (no valid biological candidate), or `retrieval_error` (search or a candidate lineage could not be retrieved) |
| `n_candidates` | Number of retained candidates |
| `lineage_depth` | Number of nodes in the selected lineage |
| `lineage` | Stored root-to-tip lineage |
| `ranks` | Rank of every lineage node (missing for unranked nodes) |
| `candidates` | Candidate table used by the decision |

### `taxo_from_lineages()`

```text
R:      taxo_from_lineages(lineages, ids = NULL, source = "user-supplied",
                           ranks = NULL)
Python: taxo_from_lineages(lineages, ids=None, source="user-supplied",
                           ranks=None)
Julia:  taxo_from_lineages(lineages; ids=nothing, source="user-supplied",
                           ranks=nothing)
```

Creates an auditable resolution from named, root-to-tip lineages without network access: a named list in R, a dictionary in Python, and a vector of `label => lineage` pairs (or an ordered dictionary) in Julia. A plain Julia `Dict` has no defined order, so its labels are sorted and positional `ids` are rejected. Optional identifiers must be unique and complete; otherwise deterministic custom identifiers `custom:<label>` are generated. Optional `ranks` give the rank of every node, aligned with the lineages (missing for unranked nodes); they are needed only by `metric = "ranked"`.

**Returns:** the same resolution type produced by `taxo_resolve()`, with every valid input marked `resolved` and source provenance retained.

### `taxo_bundle()`

```text
R:      taxo_bundle(taxa, ambiguity = "warn", verbose = FALSE,
                    progress = TRUE, within = NULL, metric = "reciprocal")
Python: taxo_bundle(taxa, ambiguity="warn", verbose=False,
                    progress=True, within=None, metric="reciprocal")
Julia:  taxo_bundle(taxa; ambiguity="warn", verbose=false,
                    progress=true, within=nothing, metric="reciprocal")
```

Combines a resolution object, its distance matrix under `metric`, source metadata, software metadata, and the metric definition. `taxa` may be raw names or an existing resolution; the remaining arguments are passed to `taxo_resolve()` for names.

**Returns:** `taxodist_bundle` in R or `TaxodistBundle` in Python and Julia.

### `write_taxodist_bundle()` / `read_taxodist_bundle()`

```text
R:      write_taxodist_bundle(bundle, file, pretty = TRUE)
        read_taxodist_bundle(file)
Python: write_taxodist_bundle(bundle, file, pretty=True)
        read_taxodist_bundle(file)
Julia:  write_taxodist_bundle(bundle, file; pretty=true)
        read_taxodist_bundle(file)
```

Writes or reads the shared JSON bundle schema, currently version 1.1, which records the metric (and, for `"ranked"`, its rank levels) and the lineage ranks. Schema 1.0 bundles are still read and must use the reciprocal metric. Readers and writers validate structure, statuses, candidate counts, lineage depths, labels, matrix symmetry, and agreement between distances and stored lineages under the stored metric. Using a bundle (printing it or passing it to `distance_matrix()`) checks its structure only and does not recompute the distances.

Bundle JSON is cross-language; cache files are not. Missing distances use JSON `null`, while disconnected infinities use `"Infinity"` or `"-Infinity"`.

### `compare_bundles()`

```text
R:      compare_bundles(old, new, tolerance = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps))
Python: compare_bundles(old, new, tolerance=sqrt(eps))
Julia:  compare_bundles(old, new; tolerance=sqrt(eps(Float64)))
```

Compares two bundles, or two bundle files, for example the same analysis repeated after the source classification was updated. Each input label is classified as `unchanged`, `added`, `removed`, `status_changed`, `id_changed`, or `lineage_changed`.

**Returns:** a comparison object with a `taxa` table (input, change, statuses, identifiers, and lineage depths in both bundles), a `distances` table of pairs present in both bundles whose distance changed, and the two creation timestamps. Printing it summarizes the changes.

## Distance computation

### `taxo_distance()`

```text
R:      taxo_distance(taxon_a, taxon_b, verbose = FALSE, metric = "reciprocal")
Python: taxo_distance(taxon_a, taxon_b, verbose=False, metric="reciprocal")
Julia:  taxo_distance(taxon_a, taxon_b; verbose=false, metric="reciprocal")
```

Retrieves both ordered lineages and, with the default metric, computes

$$
d(A,B)=
\begin{cases}
0, & L_A = L_B, \\
1 / \operatorname{depth}(\operatorname{MRCA}), & L_A \neq L_B,
\end{cases}
$$

where $L_A$ and $L_B$ are the complete ordered lineages.

MRCA detection uses only the continuous common prefix from the root. Distinct ancestor–descendant nodes therefore retain a positive distance. Root depth is 1, so distinct valid Taxonomicon nodes have distances in $(0,1]$. Infinite distance is retained as a defensive result for disconnected input lineages.

With $h$ the MRCA depth and $d_A$, $d_B$ the lineage depths (numbers of nodes, root included), the available metrics are:

| `metric` | Distance | Properties |
|---|---|---|
| `"reciprocal"` (default) | $1/h$ | Ultrametric; weights shallow divergences heavily |
| `"path"` | $d_A + d_B - 2h$ | Number of edges between the nodes; a tree metric, not an ultrametric when depths differ |
| `"wu_palmer"` | $1 - 2h/(d_A + d_B)$ | In $[0,1)$; normalizes for uneven resolution; not guaranteed to satisfy the triangle inequality |
| `"ranked"` | Half the path length through the standard Linnaean ranks only | Clarke and Warwick's step weights: 1 for congeneric species, 2 for confamilial, ...; requires lineage ranks |

Every metric is zero for identical lineages. Lineages without a shared root have infinite distance, except under `"wu_palmer"`, where their distance is 1. The `"ranked"` metric reduces both lineages to the root, the nodes whose rank is one of the configured rank levels (by default kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species), and the terminal node.

**Returns:** an S3 list in R, `dict` in Python, or named tuple in Julia with:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `distance` | Numeric hierarchy distance |
| `mrca` | MRCA name, or missing when no root is shared |
| `mrca_depth` | Number of nodes from root through the MRCA |
| `depth_a`, `depth_b` | Complete lineage depths |
| `taxon_a`, `taxon_b` | Input labels |
| `metric` | Metric used |

Returns `NULL`/`None` if either lineage cannot be retrieved.

### `mrca()`

```text
R:      mrca(taxon_a, taxon_b, verbose = FALSE)
Python: mrca(taxon_a, taxon_b, verbose=False)
Julia:  mrca(taxon_a, taxon_b; verbose=false)
```

Returns only the MRCA name from `taxo_distance()`. The result is `NULL`/`None` if retrieval fails or the lineages share no ancestor.

### `distance_matrix()`

```text
R:      distance_matrix(taxa, verbose = FALSE, progress = TRUE,
                        metric = "reciprocal")
Python: distance_matrix(taxa, verbose=False, progress=True,
                        metric="reciprocal")
Julia:  distance_matrix(taxa; verbose=false, progress=true,
                        metric="reciprocal")
```

Retrieves each lineage once and computes all pairwise distances under `metric`. Input order and labels are preserved. Unresolved taxa receive missing off-diagonal comparisons; the diagonal is zero.

**Returns:** a `dist` object in R, symmetric `pandas.DataFrame` in Python, or labeled `TaxonomicDistanceMatrix` in Julia. The metric is recorded in the `"method"` attribute of the `dist` object (which `stats::hclust()` reports), in `attrs["metric"]` in Python, and in the `metric` field in Julia. Empty input returns a correctly shaped empty object.

`taxa` may also be a resolution, whose stored lineages (and ranks) are reused, or a bundle, whose stored matrix is returned. Distances are computed from integer identifiers of each node's complete path from the root, which gives the same values as `taxo_distance()` for every pair.

### `cross_distances()`

```text
R:      cross_distances(x, y, verbose = FALSE, progress = TRUE,
                        metric = "reciprocal")
Python: cross_distances(x, y, verbose=False, progress=True,
                        metric="reciprocal")
Julia:  cross_distances(x, y; verbose=false, progress=true,
                        metric="reciprocal")
```

Computes the distances from every taxon in `x` to every taxon in `y` without computing the full square matrix of the combined set. `x` and `y` may be names, resolutions, or bundles.

**Returns:** a numeric matrix in R, `pandas.DataFrame` in Python, or labeled `TaxonomicCrossDistances` in Julia, with rows for `x` and columns for `y`. Unresolved taxa receive missing values; taxa without a common root receive infinite distance.

### `focal_distances()`

```text
R:      focal_distances(focal, community, verbose = FALSE, progress = TRUE,
                        metric = "reciprocal")
Python: focal_distances(focal, community, verbose=False, progress=True,
                        metric="reciprocal")
Julia:  focal_distances(focal, community; verbose=false, progress=true,
                        metric="reciprocal")
```

Computes the distance from one focal taxon to each community member and sorts finite results from smallest to largest.

**Returns:** a data frame with columns `taxon`, `distance`, `mrca`, and `mrca_depth` (in Julia, a named tuple with the focal label and the data frame in its `data` field). The focal name is retained as object metadata. Returns `NULL`/`None`/`nothing` if the focal lineage is unavailable.

### `closest_relative()`

```text
R:      closest_relative(taxon, candidates, verbose = FALSE,
                         metric = "reciprocal")
Python: closest_relative(taxon, candidates, verbose=False,
                         metric="reciprocal")
Julia:  closest_relative(taxon, candidates; verbose=false,
                         metric="reciprocal")
```

Ranks candidate taxa by distance from the query taxon.

**Returns:** a data frame with columns `taxon` and `distance`, sorted ascending with missing values last. Returns `NULL`/`None` if the query lineage is unavailable.

### `lineage_depth()`

```text
R:      lineage_depth(taxon, verbose = FALSE)
Python: lineage_depth(taxon, verbose=False)
Julia:  lineage_depth(taxon; verbose=false)
```

Returns the number of nodes in the retrieved lineage, including root and queried node. This is classification resolution, not elapsed time.

### `check_coverage()`

```text
R:      check_coverage(taxa, verbose = FALSE)
Python: check_coverage(taxa, verbose=False)
Julia:  check_coverage(taxa; verbose=false)
```

Checks whether each input can be resolved to a Taxonomicon identifier.

**Returns:** a named logical vector in R, nullable Boolean `pandas.Series` in Python, or a `DataFrame` with columns `taxon` and `covered` in Julia. Values are true (found), false (absent), or unknown when the server could not be reached (`NA`, `pd.NA`, or `missing`).

## Lineage comparison and membership

### `compare_lineages()`

```text
R:      compare_lineages(taxon_a, taxon_b, verbose = FALSE)
Python: compare_lineages(taxon_a, taxon_b, verbose=False)
Julia:  compare_lineages(taxon_a, taxon_b; verbose=false)
```

Prints the common lineage and the nodes unique to each side after divergence.

**Returns:** invisibly in R, and directly in Python, an object containing `lineage_a`, `lineage_b`, and `mrca_depth`.

### `shared_clades()`

```text
R:      shared_clades(taxon_a, taxon_b, verbose = FALSE)
Python: shared_clades(taxon_a, taxon_b, verbose=False)
Julia:  shared_clades(taxon_a, taxon_b; verbose=false)
```

Returns the continuous common prefix from root through the MRCA. A pair with no common ancestor returns an empty vector/list; failed retrieval returns `NULL`/`None`.

### `taxo_path()`

```text
R:      taxo_path(taxon_a, taxon_b, verbose = FALSE)
Python: taxo_path(taxon_a, taxon_b, verbose=False)
Julia:  taxo_path(taxon_a, taxon_b; verbose=false)
```

Constructs the route from taxon A upward to the MRCA and downward to taxon B.

**Returns:** a data frame with one row per node and columns:

- `node`: hierarchy node name;
- `depth`: depth in the complete lineage;
- `direction`: `"a"`, `"mrca"`, or `"b"`.

The input labels are retained as object metadata. Returns `NULL`/`None` if retrieval fails or no common ancestor exists.

### `is_member()`

```text
R:      is_member(taxon, clade, verbose = FALSE)
Python: is_member(taxon, clade, verbose=False)
Julia:  is_member(taxon, clade; verbose=false)
```

Tests whether the complete clade name occurs in the taxon's lineage. Matching is exact, case-insensitive, and ignores surrounding whitespace.

**Returns:** logical/Boolean, or `NULL`/`None` if the taxon cannot be retrieved.

### `filter_clade()`

```text
R:      filter_clade(taxa, clade, verbose = FALSE)
Python: filter_clade(taxa, clade, verbose=False)
Julia:  filter_clade(taxa, clade; verbose=false)
```

Returns only input taxa for which `is_member()` is true. Unresolved taxa are omitted.

## Taxonomic diversity and distinctness

### `taxo_distinctness()`

```text
R:      taxo_distinctness(comm, d = NULL, metric = "ranked",
                          verbose = FALSE, progress = TRUE)
Python: taxo_distinctness(comm, d=None, metric="ranked",
                          verbose=False, progress=True)
Julia:  taxo_distinctness(comm, d=nothing; metric="ranked", verbose=false,
                          progress=true, taxa=nothing, samples=nothing)
```

Computes the indices of Warwick and Clarke for one or more samples: taxonomic diversity $\Delta$, taxonomic distinctness $\Delta^*$, average taxonomic distinctness $\Delta^+$, and variation in taxonomic distinctness $\Lambda^+$. With $x_i$ the abundance of taxon $i$, $n=\sum x_i$, $S$ the number of taxa present, and $\omega_{ij}$ the distance between taxa $i$ and $j$, sums running over pairs $i<j$:

$$
\Delta = \frac{\sum\sum \omega_{ij} x_i x_j}{n(n-1)/2}, \qquad
\Delta^* = \frac{\sum\sum \omega_{ij} x_i x_j}{\sum\sum x_i x_j},
$$

$$
\Delta^+ = \frac{\sum\sum \omega_{ij}}{S(S-1)/2}, \qquad
\Lambda^+ = \frac{\sum\sum (\omega_{ij}-\Delta^+)^2}{S(S-1)/2}.
$$

`comm` is a vector of taxon names (one sample, presence only), a named vector, dictionary, or series of abundances (one sample), or a matrix or data frame with one row per sample and one column per taxon. In Julia, a numeric matrix takes its taxon names from `taxa` and its sample names from `samples`. `d` is a distance matrix whose labels include every taxon present; when omitted, it is computed with `distance_matrix()` under `metric`. The default `"ranked"` metric reproduces the classical indices based on Linnaean ranks; the other metrics use the full resolution of the classification. With presence-only data, $\Delta$ and $\Delta^*$ equal $\Delta^+$. Results agree with `vegan::taxondive()`.

**Returns:** one row per sample with columns `sample`, `S`, `Delta`, `Delta_star`, `Delta_plus`, `Lambda_plus`, and `SDelta_plus` ($S\Delta^+$): a `taxodist_distinctness` data frame in R, a `pandas.DataFrame` with `attrs["metric"]` in Python, and a named tuple `(metric, data)` in Julia. Indices are missing for samples with fewer than two taxa or when a distance between present taxa is missing or infinite.

### `taxo_distinctness_test()`

```text
R:      taxo_distinctness_test(sample, d, n_iter = 999)
Python: taxo_distinctness_test(sample, d, n_iter=999, seed=None)
Julia:  taxo_distinctness_test(sample, d; n_iter=999,
                               rng=Random.default_rng())
```

Compares $\Delta^+$ and $\Lambda^+$ of a sample (a vector of taxon names) with their distribution in `n_iter` random samples of the same number of taxa drawn without replacement from the master list (species pool) represented by `d`. The expected $\Delta^+$ is the mean distance over all pairs of the master list; the expected $\Lambda^+$ is the mean of the simulated values. A $\Delta^+$ below the lower limit indicates that the sample is less taxonomically distinct than expected from the pool. For reproducible results, use `set.seed()` in R, `seed` in Python, and `rng` in Julia; the random draws differ between languages.

**Returns:** an object with `statistics` (rows `Delta_plus` and `Lambda_plus`; columns `observed`, `expected`, `lower` and `upper` — the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the random samples — and the one-sided permutation p-values `p_lower` and `p_upper`), `simulated` (the simulated values), and the settings `S`, `pool_size`, `n_iter`, and `metric`. R returns class `taxodist_distinctness_test`, Python `TaxodistDistinctnessTest`, and Julia a named tuple.

## Multivariate analysis and visualization

### `taxo_cluster()`

```text
R:      taxo_cluster(taxa, method = "average", ...)
Python: taxo_cluster(taxa, method="average", **kwargs)
Julia:  taxo_cluster(taxa; method="average", kwargs...)
```

Accepts taxon names, a resolution, a bundle, or a previously computed distance object. Further arguments, including `metric`, are passed to `distance_matrix()` when the distances must be computed. The default is average-linkage hierarchical clustering.

**Returns:**

- R: a `taxodist_cluster` list with `hclust` and `dist`;
- Python: a dictionary with `hclust` (SciPy linkage matrix) and `dist`;
- Julia: a named tuple with `hclust` (`Clustering.Hclust`), `dist`, and `method`.

If the matrix contains missing or infinite values, or represents fewer than two taxa, clustering is skipped and `hclust` is `NULL`/`None`.

### `taxo_ordinate()`

```text
R:      taxo_ordinate(taxa, k = 2, ...)
Python: taxo_ordinate(taxa, k=2, **kwargs)
Julia:  taxo_ordinate(taxa; k=2, kwargs...)
```

Performs classical multidimensional scaling (PCoA). The requested `k` must be a positive integer and is reduced to at most $n-1$. Further arguments, including `metric`, are passed to `distance_matrix()` when the distances must be computed.

**Returns:** an S3 list or dictionary with `points`, `dist`, `GOF`, and `eig`. Invalid matrices return the same structure with empty analysis components.

### `taxo_heatmap()`

```text
R:      taxo_heatmap(taxa, ..., verbose = FALSE, progress = TRUE,
                     metric = "reciprocal")
Python: taxo_heatmap(taxa, verbose=False, progress=True,
                     metric="reciprocal", **kwargs)
Julia:  taxo_heatmap(taxa; display_plot=true, verbose=false,
                     progress=true, metric="reciprocal", kwargs...)
```

Plots the distance matrix with clustered rows and columns. Additional arguments are passed only to the plotting function: `stats::heatmap()` in R, `seaborn.clustermap()` in Python (overriding the defaults `cmap` and `annot`), and `Plots.heatmap()` in Julia. `verbose`, `progress`, and `metric` control the computation of the matrix when names are supplied.

Plotting in Python requires the optional dependencies (`pip install "taxodist[plot]"`); in Julia, plotting is enabled by `using Plots`.

**Returns:** the underlying `dist` object invisibly in R, `pandas.DataFrame` in Python, or `TaxonomicDistanceMatrix` in Julia. Plotting is skipped for incomplete, infinite, or undersized matrices.

### `taxo_tree()`

```text
R:      taxo_tree(taxa, verbose = FALSE, progress = TRUE)
Python: taxo_tree(taxa, verbose=False, progress=True)
Julia:  taxo_tree(taxa; verbose=false, progress=true)
```

Builds a tree directly from the lineages of names, a resolution, or a bundle. Internal nodes are the named clades at which the supplied taxa diverge; clades with a single descendant are collapsed, and polytomies are retained. A clade at depth $h$ is placed at height $1/(2h)$ and tips at height zero, so the tree is ultrametric and its patristic distances equal `distance_matrix()`. Taxa with identical lineages are joined by zero-length branches; a taxon that is an ancestor of another supplied taxon is attached to its clade node. All lineages must share the same root; taxa without a lineage are dropped with a warning.

**Returns:** an `ape`-compatible `phylo` object in R; a `TaxodistTree` in Python (with `to_newick()` and `cophenetic()`) and in Julia (with `newick(tree)` and `cophenetic(tree)`). Tip labels are input labels and node labels are clade names.

::: {.callout-warning title="Interpretation of analysis output"}
Clustering, PCoA, and heatmaps summarize the supplied classification-depth distances. They do not infer phylogenetic history or evolutionary branch lengths.
:::

## Cache management

### `cache_info()`

```text
cache_info()
```

Prints and returns counts of cached lineages and identifiers, the names of the cached taxa with their identifiers, and approximate memory use. The return fields are `n_lineages`, `n_ids`, `taxa`, `ids`, and `size_bytes`.

### `save_cache()`

```text
R:      save_cache(file = NULL)
Python: save_cache(file=None)
Julia:  save_cache(file=nothing)
```

Serializes the current cache to an R `.rds`, Python `.pkl`, or Julia `.json` file. Without a file, a persistent per-user location is used: `tools::R_user_dir("taxodist", "cache")` in R and the platform's user cache directory in Python and Julia (overridable with `TAXODIST_CACHE_DIR`). Returns the path of the written file (invisibly in R).

### `load_cache()`

```text
R:      load_cache(file = NULL)
Python: load_cache(file=None)
Julia:  load_cache(file=nothing)
```

Validates and restores a previously saved cache, by default from the persistent per-user location. Validation occurs before the active cache is modified. The R, Python, and Julia cache files are not interchangeable.

`save_cache()` records the version of the lineage parser in the file. Lineages from cache files written before version 1.0.0, whose parser could produce malformed nodes, are discarded on loading with a warning; their taxon identifiers are kept.

::: {.callout-warning title="Python cache security"}
Python cache files use `pickle`. Only load `.pkl` files from trusted sources, because unpickling untrusted data can execute arbitrary code.
:::

### `clear_cache()`

```text
clear_cache()
```

Removes all identifiers and lineages cached in the current session. Returns invisibly `NULL` in R, `None` in Python, and `nothing` in Julia.

## Packaged reference data

### `taxobase` / `load_taxobase()`

```text
R:      data(taxobase, package = "taxodist")
Python: taxobase = load_taxobase()
Julia:  taxobase = load_taxobase()
```

Loads the fixed reference object distributed with the packages. Its metadata record the generation date and package version; the version 1.0.0 object was rebuilt with the new lineage parser. Components include taxa, coverage, lineages, pairwise examples, search results, general and statistical distance matrices, and provenance metadata.

R stores distance components as `dist`; Python converts matrices to labeled `pandas.DataFrame` objects; Julia converts them to labeled `TaxonomicDistanceMatrix` objects.

## Display helpers

R uses S3 methods for distance results, focal results, paths, clusters, ordinations, resolutions, bundles, bundle comparisons, and distinctness results. Python exposes corresponding explicit helpers: `print_taxodist_result()`, `print_focal_distances()`, `print_taxodist_path()`, `print_taxodist_distinctness()`, `plot_taxodist_cluster()`, `plot_taxodist_ord()`, and `summary_taxodist_ord()`. Julia provides `plot_taxodist_cluster()`, `plot_taxodist_ord()`, and `summary_taxodist_ord()` alongside native display of named tuples, data frames, and labeled matrices. The plotting helpers need `pip install "taxodist[plot]"` in Python and `using Plots` in Julia.

For complete argument documentation in R, run `help(package = "taxodist")`. In Python, use `help(taxodist.function_name)`. In Julia, use help mode, for example `?taxo_distance`.
